one_liner: Managed .NET decoder for Targa and DDS (BC1-BC7) images; beats FreeImage, DevIL and Magick.NET called from C#.
what_it_does: Pfim is a .NET Standard 2.0 library that decodes TGA (raw, RLE, color-mapped) and DDS (uncompressed, DXT1/3/5, BC4-BC7, R16F/R32F) into a raw byte[] plus width, height, stride and an ImageFormat tag, with DDS mipmaps exposed as offsets into the same buffer. Entry points are Pfimage.FromFile/FromStream (format sniffed from the header) or Targa.Create/Dds.Create on a byte[] or Stream. It does not produce a Bitmap or texture itself: the README and sample projects show the glue for GDI+, WPF, MonoGame, SkiaSharp and ImageSharp. It is not a drop-in for FreeImage, DevIL or ImageMagick, which cover far more formats and also encode.
how_it_is_fast: For RLE Targa read from a byte[] or publicly visible MemoryStream, an unsafe pointer loop (CompressedTarga.FastPass) expands run packets with 32-bit stores (Util.memset) and a three-int rotation trick for 24-bit pixels (RunLength3), and copies raw packets with Buffer.MemoryCopy; uncompressed Targa is a row-by-row Buffer.BlockCopy that only flips row order. DDS blocks are decoded one 4x4 block at a time with plain scalar C# (no SIMD; since 0.11.0 the color interpolation uses float lerp). Output buffers can come from a caller-supplied IImageAllocator (for example ArrayPool), which the benchmarks use. Much of the measured gap is the competitors' cost of going through .NET interop wrappers and converting to their own pixel formats, not a faster block-decode algorithm.
when_to_use: C# or Unity/MonoGame/Xamarin code that must read .tga or .dds assets without shipping native FreeImage, DevIL or ImageMagick binaries.
Bulk loading of many small game textures or sprites, where per-call fixed cost and GC pressure dominate and a pooled IImageAllocator can be reused across decodes.
Tools that need DDS metadata or the still-compressed BC payload (PfimConfig decompress: false) to upload to the GPU directly.
Pipelines that want raw BGR(A) bytes with a 4-byte-aligned stride for GDI+, WPF or SkiaSharp interop.
when_not_to_use: Anything beyond TGA and DDS: no PNG, JPEG, WebP, KTX or encoding (DDS encoding is only an open PR, #131).
Untrusted TGA input: the RLE fast path writes runs and reads input through raw pointers with no bounds checks (see gotchas).
Volume (3D) DDS textures, which decode only the first slice (open issue #110), or the DDS files reported unreadable in open issue #107.
Top-right or bottom-right oriented TGA files, which are decoded as bottom-left without the horizontal flip (release notes 0.6.0, open issue #38).
Choosing a texture decoder on speed from the published numbers: they come from a 2019 run on one 120x120, four-color image and pre-fix DXT code.

integration.min_toolchain: .NET Standard 2.0 (.NET Framework 4.6.1+, .NET Core 2.0+ or Mono/Unity with netstandard2.0); unsafe code is compiled into the package
integration.platforms: any .NET runtime with netstandard2.0 support (Windows, Linux, macOS, mobile through Xamarin)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the Targa decoders are stateless static singletons in current code, and a shared IImageAllocator must itself be thread-safe (ArrayPool.Shared is)

gotchas: Use DataLen, not Data.Length: pooled buffers can be larger than the image and DDS mipmaps share the buffer; Dispose the image to return buffers to a custom allocator.
Despite the Rgb24/Rgba32 names, bytes are in B,G,R(,A) order as stored in TGA (the README maps Rgba32 to GDI+ Format32bppArgb); there is no channel swap pass.

Possible memory-safety bug from reading the code: CompressedTarga.FastPass and RunLength write each RLE run with pointer stores without checking the row or buffer end, and FastPass reads the input pointer without checking the input length, so a crafted or truncated RLE TGA (or one whose runs cross scanlines, which TGA 2.0 forbids) can write past the output array or read past the input array.

DXT1 output changed from 24-bit RGB to 32-bit RGBA in 0.10.0, and DXT1/3/5 interpolation changed to float lerp in 0.11.0 to fix systematic rounding errors (issue #88, PR #98); code written against older versions sees different formats and pixel values.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No catalogued sibling decodes TGA or DDS in managed .NET: bc7enc, bc7e, icbc, Goofy and etcpak are C/C++ texture encoders, and the rest are PNG/JPEG/QOI codecs. Pick Pfim to read BC-compressed DDS or TGA from C# without native code; use those siblings to produce BC/ETC textures, and a C/C++ BCn decoder when you can ship native code.
verified_claims_summary: BenchmarkDotNet 0.11.5 on .NET Framework 4.6.1 (Clr, RyuJit, x64, CPU not recorded), April 2019 (commit 6bdf779): decoding one 120x120 image from an in-memory byte[], Pfim with a pooled allocator took 5.1 us for 24-bit RLE TGA versus 65.8 us for FreeImage and 47.8 us for DevILSharp (12.9x and 9.4x), and 1.6 us versus 115 us for DevILSharp on uncompressed 32-bit DDS, but only 1.61x faster than FreeImage on DXT1, 1.16x on DXT3 and 1.1% slower on DXT5. The test image has only 4 distinct colors, so each RLE file is 240 run packets (two 60-pixel runs per row) and no raw packets, Pfim's best case, and the uncompressed paths are a single Buffer.BlockCopy (row-flipped for TGA) of 57,600 bytes, while the competitors pay .NET interop costs and convert to their own pixel formats.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-07-15, release 0.11.4 on 2025-11-29, benchmark project moved to net8.0 but not re-run), MIT-licensed and on NuGet; copyable, but the published speed numbers predate the DXT correctness fixes and should be re-measured before relying on them.
